Lindiwe was fifteen and the only one in her Cape Town class who stayed after school for cello. The boys called her "Grandma Music" and hummed funeral tunes when she walked past with the case.
One afternoon her friend Tariq caught up with her at the bus stop. "Why don't you just play guitar? People would think you're cool."
Lindiwe shifted the heavy case on her back. "When I play Bach, it's like the music knows what I'm feeling before I do. Guitar doesn't do that for me."
"Even with the jokes?"
"The jokes sting," she admitted. "But if I quit, I'd be giving away the only thing that feels like mine."
Tariq was quiet. Then he said, "Play me something on Saturday?"

qa.q: What did the boys call Lindiwe?
qa.a: They called her "Grandma Music".

qa.q: How does Lindiwe feel about the jokes and about the cello?
qa.a: The jokes sting and hurt, but she feels the cello is truly hers and that the music understands her, so her love of it is stronger than her wish to fit in.

qa.q: What could help Lindiwe keep going despite the teasing?
qa.a: Friends like Tariq who take interest, and perhaps other young musicians, can support her while she keeps choosing what feels true.

qa.q: How does Tariq's view of Lindiwe's music change?
qa.a: He first suggests guitar to look cool, but after hearing why she plays he becomes curious and asks her to play for him.

grounding: A teenager keeps learning classical cello despite classmates' jokes because it feels true to her, valuing that over fitting in.

At the boys' hostel in Chandigarh, Raghav practised his Hindustani vocals every morning at six in the music room. His roommates called it "the alarm clock" and some did loud imitations in the corridor.
One evening Devika Ma'am, the music teacher, found him alone, practising a raag for the fifth time.
"The others tease you, don't they?"
Raghav shrugged. "They're right that it's not cool. Everyone else listens to rap."
"So why do you continue?"
He thought for a moment. "When I sing this raag, I feel like I'm actually me. Not trying to be like anyone."
Devika Ma'am nodded. "There's a youth music festival in March. Would you like to try?"
Raghav's face lit up. "Yes."

qa.q: At what time did Raghav practise every morning?
qa.a: He practised every morning at six.

qa.q: What does Raghav mean when he says he feels like 'actually me' while singing?
qa.a: He feels true to himself and at peace when singing, so the joy of it outweighs the embarrassment of being teased.

qa.q: How could Devika Ma'am help Raghav keep growing?
qa.a: She can keep encouraging him, guide his practice and give chances like the festival, so his interest has room to grow.

qa.q: How might the roommates see Raghav's early practice?
qa.a: They find it odd and noisy, joking about it as an alarm clock, without seeing what it means to him.

grounding: A teenager keeps practising classical vocals despite hostel teasing because it feels true to him.

Dear Thomas Sir,
You asked in class why I still go for Carnatic veena lessons on Saturdays when the others go to the mall. I didn't answer then, so I'm writing it.
My friends think it's old-fashioned. Some of them send me songs with "aunty music 😅" as a joke. It used to make me want to quit.
But when I play, I lose track of time. My fingers find things my mouth can't say. It's the only place I don't feel like I'm acting.
So I've decided to keep going, even if it's never cool. I wanted you to know, because you're the one teacher who didn't laugh.
Thank you,
Minakshi

qa.q: What instrument does Minakshi play?
qa.a: Minakshi plays the Carnatic veena.

qa.q: How has Minakshi felt about the teasing, and what has changed?
qa.a: The jokes used to hurt and made Minakshi want to quit, but now Minakshi feels that playing is more true than fitting in, and has decided to keep going.

qa.q: How could Thomas Sir respond to this letter in a supportive way?
qa.a: Thomas Sir could thank Minakshi, show interest in the music, and perhaps offer a chance to perform or share it in class.

qa.q: How might Minakshi's friends see the Saturday lessons differently if they heard the letter?
qa.a: They might realise the lessons are not old-fashioned for Minakshi but the one place of feeling real, and joke less.

grounding: A teenager keeps learning veena despite friends' jokes because it feels true, choosing inner interest over fitting in.

Sahil's bus back to the town of Karad was full of students, and he sat by the window with the offer letter in his bag. A famous software company in Bengaluru. The whole village had heard.
At home, his father was already telling neighbours. His friend Nazia met him at the tea stall. "So when do you leave?"
"I'm not going."
She put her cup down. "Sahil!"
"I'm joining the farmers' water project here. Less money. No one's heard of it." His voice shook. "I kept imagining the office, and I felt like a stranger in my own life. When I walk the canal with the water team, I feel like me."
"Your father?"
"I'll tell him tonight. I'm scared. But I'm also, strangely, calm."
Nazia looked at him for a long time. "Then go and tell him."

qa.q: Where was the famous software company?
qa.a: The famous software company was in Bengaluru.

qa.q: What is Sahil feeling as he tells Nazia his choice?
qa.a: He is scared, with a shaking voice, but also strangely calm, because the water project fits who he is.

qa.q: What would you advise Sahil for the talk with his father tonight?
qa.a: Explain honestly why the water project fits his values, listen to his father's worries, and stay kind even if his father is upset.

qa.q: How might Sahil's father feel when he hears the news tonight?
qa.a: His father may feel disappointed and embarrassed after telling the neighbours, and worried about Sahil's future.

grounding: A young adult turns down a famous, well-paid job for local work that fits his values, feeling both fear and calm.

On a grey morning in Hanoi, Bao stood outside the glass tower where he'd been offered a job at an international bank. His cousin Santiago, visiting from Mexico City, had come for moral support.
"You look sick," Santiago said.
"I'm going in to say no."
"No? You said the salary was huge."
"It is." Bao pulled his jacket tighter. "But last month I volunteered at the street children's centre. I've been going every weekend. I want to work there full time."
"And the bank?"
"Every time I thought about it, I felt proud, and then nothing. At the centre I feel tired and alive."
He went in. Twenty minutes later he came out, pale but smiling. "Done. I'm terrified. And I feel light."

qa.q: Where did Bao volunteer every weekend?
qa.a: He volunteered at the street children's centre.

qa.q: How does Bao feel after saying no to the bank?
qa.a: He feels terrified and light at the same time: frightened of the choice, but calm that it fits him.

qa.q: What might help Bao through the first months of this new path?
qa.a: Keeping in touch with supportive people like Santiago and reminding himself why the centre feels right when the fear comes.

qa.q: How is Santiago affected by watching Bao make this choice?
qa.a: Santiago moves from surprise at turning down a huge salary to seeing Bao's relief, and likely comes to respect the decision.

grounding: A young adult turns down a prestigious, well-paid bank job for work that fits his values, feeling both fear and calm.

Week one: Dr Jyoti, who ran the college botany lab, noticed first-year Jahnavi staying back after practicals, peering at moss under the microscope long after the class had left. The practical wasn't even graded.
Week four: Jahnavi was there again at seven in the evening, sketching leaf cells in a notebook of her own. "Ma'am, is it okay if I use this microscope? I just want to see more."
Dr Jyoti felt a small warmth she hadn't felt in years of teaching. She gave Jahnavi a spare key and old research journals.
Week ten: Jahnavi's parents called, asking whether botany would lead to a good job. Dr Jyoti said, "Let her explore for now. She's genuinely alive in that lab. I'd hate to rush her into a box."

qa.q: What was Jahnavi sketching in her own notebook?
qa.a: She was sketching leaf cells.

qa.q: What did Dr Jyoti feel on seeing Jahnavi in the lab at seven in the evening?
qa.a: She felt a small warmth she hadn't felt in years, delighted to see a student so truly interested.

qa.q: What did Dr Jyoti do well as a mentor?
qa.a: She gave Jahnavi space and tools, a spare key and research journals, and told her parents to let her explore instead of rushing her toward a set career.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi's parents see her staying late in the lab?
qa.a: They may feel anxious about whether it leads to a good job, wanting security for her future.

grounding: A mentor notices a student staying late out of real interest and gives her space and tools instead of pushing her toward a career.

"Bhavna, you ask why I let the new interns choose their own projects. I learned that from one boy.
I, Chaitanya, was a young man of twenty-two, an engineer, when I first mentored interns at the bus depot workshop. One boy, Iqbal, was supposed to learn engine servicing. But every lunch break I found him drawing little seat designs in a notebook, measuring passengers' knees.
Once, I stayed late and found him there at nine at night, building a seat model from cardboard. He wasn't paid overtime. He wasn't being marked.
I could have told him to stick to engines. Instead I gave him a corner of the workshop and scrap metal. Two years later his seat was in forty buses.
When a young person lights up like that, you stand back and hand them tools."

qa.q: What was Iqbal building at nine at night?
qa.a: He was building a seat model from cardboard.

qa.q: How did young Chaitanya feel when he found Iqbal working late?
qa.a: He felt curious and moved, seeing that Iqbal was working from real interest, not for pay or marks.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Chaitanya chose to give Iqbal a workshop corner and scrap metal instead of pushing him back to engines, which let his interest grow into a real design.

qa.q: How might Iqbal have felt when he was given his own workshop corner?
qa.a: Iqbal was probably thrilled and encouraged, feeling seen for what he truly loved.

grounding: An elder recalls, as a young mentor, noticing an intern light up and stay late for his own interest, and giving him tools instead of pressure.

The college theatre club had only one working light and three days before the play, and Jagdish, the club's faculty mentor, was already exhausted. Then he noticed Hansa.
She wasn't acting. She was on a ladder with a torch, rigging coloured paper over the one light to make it look like sunset. She had stayed after rehearsal every night, though lighting earned no marks.
"Hansa, you know this isn't part of your grade?"
"I know, sir. I just... want to see if it works."
Jagdish had planned to push her toward the lead role; her parents wanted her in debate for her CV. He watched her face as the light turned orange. He climbed down, found some old gels in the storeroom and handed them to her. "Your stage," he said.

qa.q: What was Hansa rigging over the one light?
qa.a: She was rigging coloured paper to make it look like sunset.

qa.q: How did Jagdish feel as he watched Hansa's face when the light turned orange?
qa.a: He was moved and delighted to see her genuine interest light up, which changed his plan for her.

qa.q: Why was handing Hansa the gels a wise choice?
qa.a: It gave her space and tools to follow her own interest, instead of pushing her toward the lead role or debate for her CV.

qa.q: How might Hansa's parents see her choice of lighting?
qa.a: They might worry that lighting won't help her CV, since they wanted her in debate.

grounding: A mentor notices a student staying late to rig lights from real interest and gives her tools instead of pushing her into a set role.
